The local-first database for people and agents.

Every member keeps its own copy, under its own keys. Reads never leave the device. The relay in the middle stores the changes and cannot read a byte of them.

Read the docsReview the RFCs

In design. The API below is what the RFCs decide; nothing is released yet.

Built for the data people and agents share.

Tickets, notes, customer records, shared documents. Eight situations, and what the design does in each.

Where a central database is the weaker choice

  • Erasure that reaches every copyErasing a person destroys their key, in every archive and snapshot. The audit trail survives.
  • A relay breach leaks nothing readableA copy of the relay's database is ciphertext and metadata, nothing more.
  • An outside agent, limited to one spaceIt gets one space's keys, signs every write, and loses access when you remove it.
  • A thousand agent queries a minuteAgents query their own copy: no round trip, no rate limit, no cost per read.
  • The relay goes down, work goes onEvery member keeps reading and writing. When the relay is back, every copy converges.

What you keep without a central server

  • Writing together through a tunnelRich text on Yjs: both keep typing offline, and no text is lost when they meet again.
  • Subscribe instead of pollA query on a declared index calls your app when a change may alter its page.
  • Streaming as a data typeAn agent's answer arrives chunk by chunk, over the same encrypted change stream.

Two members, one space, and a relay that sees bytes.

Here the real SDK will run in three frames and the relay in your browser. Until then, this is a simulation of what you will see.

A Setup
  1. Open the database
  2. Create the space “team chat”
  3. Add B and C as writers
B Member
C Member
R Relay log

    Install the SDK and write five calls.

    No keys in your code. The SDK creates, stores and rotates them.

    npm install @nocentraldb/sdk

    Rust: cargo add nocentraldb

    Describe the model once. ncdb model build turns it into model.lock.json.

    import { nc } from "@nocentraldb/sdk";

export const model = nc.model({
  messages: nc.collection(
    {
      text: nc.string(),
      author: nc.link("people"),
      sentAt: nc.int(),
    },
    { indexes: { bySentAt: nc.index(["sentAt"]) } },
  ),
});

    A creates this member's key on first open, then a space. No relay needed to start.

    const db = await nc.open({ model, lock, relay: "wss://relay.example.com" });

const chat = await db.spaces.create();

    B and C send an invitation: a public identity, never a key. A adds them.

    // On B and on C:
const invitation = await db.invitation();
send(invitation.toString());

// On A, an admin of the space:
await chat.members.add(nc.invitation(text), { role: "writer" });

    One write is one signed, encrypted change. It resolves before the relay has it.

    await chat.write((tx) => {
  tx.create(model.messages, { text: "Can you look at the relay draft?", sentAt: Date.now() });
});

    C reads its own copy. The listener runs at once and after every change that may alter the page.

    const latest = model.messages.indexes.bySentAt.take(50);

const stop = db.subscribe(latest, (page) => render(page.items));

    What it does not do, said plainly.

    Every guarantee names its limits. These are the ones to know before you build.

    The relay sees metadata.
    Which key is in which space, when and how much each key writes, and who reads from where. It can withhold changes.
    Removing a member keeps their copy.
    The space key rotates, so they read nothing new. What they already received stays on their device.
    Erasure has edges.
    It does not reach devices that never come back online, a modified client, exports, screenshots or unmarked free text.
    No queries on the server.
    Queries run on declared indexes in the local copy. For analytics across all users, use a central database.
    v1 is not post-quantum.
    Ciphertext recorded today could be read by a future quantum computer.
